title: Crash and Recovery Responds to A300 Civilian Airbus Crash
description: Package about how the Crash and Recovery team from the 455th Expeditionary Maintenance Group handled the crash of an A300 Civilian Airbus. Produced by Master Sgt. Sebastiano Mariano Jr. Afghanistan
keywords: 455th Expeditionary Maintenance Group, Crash and Recovery team, A300 Civilian Airbus, Alexander Figliola, Afghanistan

transcript.text: Bogram Airfield recently had an aircraft incident that slowed down runway operations.
The crew of an A-300 civilian airbus made an emergency landing on March 1st.
Upon landing, the landing gear on the left wing collapsed, forcing the aircraft into
the ditch.
The crash and recovery team from the 455th Expeditionary Maintenance Group was monitoring
the incident as it happened.
Once the plane stopped, the crash and recovery team knew their top priority, to get the runway
back to 100% operational capability.
How are we going to get this out of here?
And how bad is it blocking the runway and what are we going to use?
We just started automatically, started thinking what we need to get.
And then people started coming out, asking us what we're going to do, how we're going
to take care of the situation.
The crash and recovery team worked with other units to try and move the aircraft further
away from the runway.
This would allow full operations to continue.
Personnel from the Civil Engineer Squadron, other maintenance units, and the U.S. Army
provided assistance.
An off-base agency offered a 120-ton crane to help lift the left wing.
This would allow the trailer to go underneath the wing and provide support during the move.
Tech Sergeant Figliola tells us how he and his team were prepared for an incident like this.
Once a year at home station, we go through a training course.
A lot of it consists of actually lifting an aircraft, but at home it's in F-15.
We either lifted with airbags or we lifted with a crane.
We have instructional videos that show us several aircraft crashes and we go through
what we do to get this out of the mud or out of the dirt or whatever it is.
The biggest challenge for everyone was lifting the heavy aircraft in order to move it.
The combined effort of all personnel involved moved the aircraft to a safe distance in just
over 28 hours.
Reporting from Bagram Airfield, Afghanistan, I'm Air Force Master Sergeant Sabeschiano-Marino.
